## Where we're heading

In this and the next few weeks, you will learn to run
command-line bioinformatics programs at OSC step by step:

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

1. More general information about OSC _(this lecture)_
2. How to use software at OSC, including programs that aren't installed _(next lecture)_
3. How to write shell scripts _(next week)_
4. How to submit shell scripts as "batch jobs" _(in week 9)_
5. How to build functional commands to run such programs _(throughout)_

# Compute nodes, compute jobs, and cores {background-color="#A7B1B7"}

## Using compute nodes via "jobs"

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}

### [Compute jobs]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

You use compute nodes by **requesting resources**,
such as a number of nodes and cores, and for how long you need them.

These requests result in "**compute jobs**" (or simply "jobs").
Our VS Code sessions are an example!

:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1" style="border-left: 1px solid #A7B1B7; height: 100%; margin: 0 auto; width: 0;"></div>
:::
::: {.column width="47%" .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}

### [The job scheduler]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

Many users send requests all the time,
so a **job scheduler** (**Slurm** at OSC) considers each request
and assigns resources to jobs as they become available.

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
In week 9, you'll learn to submit scripts as "batch jobs" with Slurm.
:::

:::
:::

## Cores

In week 2, you learned that a supercomputer center has multiple supercomputers,
each of which consists of many nodes. But there is one more "level":

![](../img/terminology.png){fig-align="center" width="95%" fig-alt="A diagram showing how the terms core/processor, node, and cluster/supercomputer fit together." .lightbox}

## Cores

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}

### [What is a core?]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

A component of a computer (node) that can (semi-)independently
perform a computing task, like running a bioinformatics program.

Many programs can use **multiple cores** for a single run,
which can speed things up considerably.

:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1" style="border-left: 1px solid #A7B1B7; height: 100%; margin: 0 auto; width: 0;"></div>
:::
::: {.column width="47%" .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}

### [Core / Processor / CPU / Thread]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

These terms are not technically synonyms,
but are often used interchangeably.

For working at OSC, treat them as meaning the same thing:
the components of a node that can be reserved and used independently.

:::
:::

. . .

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Typical compute jobs use 1 node and multiple cores on that node.

A job's resource usage is measured in **core hours**.
For example, using 2 cores for 2 hours = 4 core hours.
:::

## Core hours

::: callout-quiz
::: callout-note
#### Quiz: Core hours

A) You run a program with 8 reserved cores for 3 hours.
   How many core hours will your OSC Project be billed for?

B) Afterwards, you find out that the program only ever used 1 of those cores.
   Does that change the number of billed core hours?

C) Afterwards, you find out that the program finished after 1 hour,
   and the job ended.
   Does that change the number of billed core hours?

What does this tell you about how many cores and hours to request?

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

<!-----
<details><summary> {{< fa square-check >}} &nbsp; &nbsp; _Click for the answers_</summary>

A) 8 cores × 3 hours = **24 core hours**.

B) **No**: you're billed for the cores you _reserved_, whether or not they were used.
   So request multiple cores only if the program can actually use them
   (check its documentation!) --- otherwise you waste resources
   and, as you'll see later, may also wait longer for your job to start.

C) **Yes**: OSC only bills for the time a job actually ran,
   so 8 cores × 1 hour = **8 core hours**.

**Takeaway**: Only request as many cores as the program can use.
For time, it's fine to be generous, because unused time isn't billed
(though very long requests may wait longer in the queue).

</details>

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />
------>
:::
:::

## Compute node types

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}

### ["Standard" nodes]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

- By far the most numerous (e.g., Pitzer has 564).
- Even these vary in size, e.g., from 40 to 48 cores per node on Pitzer.
- Used by default, and will serve you well for most omics analyses.

:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1" style="border-left: 1px solid #A7B1B7; height: 100%; margin: 0 auto; width: 0;"></div>
:::
::: {.column width="47%" .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}

### [Other node types]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

- Nodes with extra memory: `largemem` and `hugemem`.
- Nodes with GPUs (Graphics Processing Units) in addition to CPUs.

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
You may occasionally need these, for example for genome or transcriptome assembly
(large-memory nodes) or Oxford Nanopore base-calling (GPU nodes).
:::

:::
:::

## Memory versus storage

When we talk about a computer's **memory**, this refers to **RAM** ---
don't confuse this with file *storage*.

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%" .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}

### [Memory (RAM)]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

- The data a computer has actively "loaded" or in use.
- Accessed _orders of magnitude_ faster than data on disk.
- E.g., heavily used when you play a game or have many browser tabs open.

:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="2" style="border-left: 1px solid #A7B1B7; height: 100%; margin: 0 auto; width: 0;"></div>
:::
::: {.column width="47%" .fragment data-fragment-index="2"}

### [Storage (disk)]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

- The data that is saved in files on disk.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
When your computer freezes, it's typically because memory is full,
and it starts using disk storage as "virtual memory" --- which is much slower.
:::
:::
:::

. . .

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Bioinformatics programs may load input data into memory for fast access,
and hold intermediate results there too.
With large datasets, they may need 10s or 100s of GBs of memory.
:::

## Quiz: True or false?

::: callout-quiz
::: callout-note
#### True or false?

A) If a program crashes because it runs out of memory,
   moving your files to a location with a larger storage quota will fix it.

B) Requesting 8 cores instead of 1 will make any program run about 8× faster.

C) A file you created while connected to Pitzer can also be accessed from Cardinal.

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

<!-----
<details><summary> {{< fa square-check >}} &nbsp; &nbsp; _Click for the answers_</summary>

A) **False**: memory (RAM) is not storage.
   You would need to request more memory, possibly on a `largemem` node.

B) **False**: the program has to support using multiple cores,
   and even then, the speed-up is usually less than proportional.

C) **True**: file systems are shared among OSC's clusters.

</details>

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />
------>
:::
:::

# OSC Projects {background-color="#A7B1B7"}

## OSC bills Project-wise

OSC bills **Projects** (not individual users), and only for two things:

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="30%" .box-blue .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}
### File storage

- File storage in the Project dirs (`/fs/ess`).

- Charged per TB per month.

:::
::: {.column width="3%"}
:::
::: {.column width="30%" .box-amber .fragment data-fragment-index="2"}
### Compute

- Compute node usage

- Charged per core hour.

:::
::: {.column width="3%"}
:::
::: {.column width="30%" .box-teal .fragment data-fragment-index="3"}
### Who pays?

- Every OSU PI gets a $1,000 yearly credit.
- OSU colleges pay some or all of the costs --- CFAES currently pays all of it.

:::
:::

. . .

<br>

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Prices for academic usage are generally low, but a Project using dozens of TBs
and tens of thousands of core hours could be charged over a thousand dollars per year.
:::

## OSC Projects

In this course, we exclusively use the course's OSC Project `PAS3493`.
For your own research, you would likely use a Project specific to a research
project or grant, or your lab's general-use Project.

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%" .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}

### [Using a Project]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

In practice, "using" a Project means:

- Storing data in its `/fs/ess` and/or `/fs/scratch` dirs.
- Selecting the Project when starting compute jobs,
  like Code Server and (later in the course) batch jobs.

:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="2" style="border-left: 1px solid #A7B1B7; height: 100%; margin: 0 auto; width: 0;"></div>
:::
::: {.column width="47%" .fragment data-fragment-index="2"}

### [Managing a Project]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

Generally only done by PIs
([more info](https://www.osc.edu/supercomputing/portals/client_portal/projects_budgets_and_charge_accounts){target="_blank"}).
Project administrators can, among others:

- Manage the compute budget and `/fs/ess` storage allocation.
- Add users to the Project.

:::
:::

# Storage areas {background-color="#A7B1B7"}

## Storage areas: overview

An expanded version of the table from Week 2:

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

| Area        | Path           | Quota              | Backed up? | Auto-purged?  | One for each... |
| ------------ | -------------- | ------------------ | ---------- | ------------- | --------------- |
| **Home**     | `/users/`      | 500 GB / 1 M files | Yes        | No            | User            |

: {.striped .hover tbl-colwidths="[12, 16, 21, 15, 17, 19]"}

## Storage areas: overview

An expanded version of the table from Week 2:

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

| Area        | Path           | Quota              | Backed up? | Auto-purged?  | One for each... |
| ----------- | -------------- | ------------------ | ---------- | ------------- | --------------- |
| **Home**    | `/users/`      | 500 GB / 1 M files | Yes        | No            | User            |
| **Project** | `/fs/ess/`     | Flexible           | Yes        | No            | OSC Project     |
| **Scratch** | `/fs/scratch/` | 100 TB             | No         | After 60 days | OSC Project     |

: {.striped .hover tbl-colwidths="[12, 16, 21, 15, 17, 19]"}

. . .

<br><br>

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
There is a fourth storage area, _compute_, that is on compute nodes and is deleted
when a job ends.\
In practice, this is rarely needed in bioinformatics, and we won't use it in this course.
:::

## When are different storage areas useful?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="30%" .box-blue .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}
### Project

- **Drawbacks**: storage is billed (per TB per month),
  and I/O is slower than on Scratch.

- **Useful for**: everything you want to keep long-term and share with collaborators:
  raw data, scripts, documentation, and key results.

:::
::: {.column width="3%"}
:::
::: {.column width="30%" .box-amber .fragment data-fragment-index="2"}
### Scratch

- **Drawbacks**: temporary and not backed up.

- **Useful for**: large datasets, thanks to _effectively unlimited_ space and
  _faster_ read/write ("I/O") speed.
  Run analyses here, then copy key files to the Project dir.

:::
::: {.column width="3%"}
:::
::: {.column width="30%" .box-teal .fragment data-fragment-index="3"}
### Home

- **Drawbacks**: limited space that can't be expanded,
  and harder to share files with collaborators.

- **Useful for**: files you use across projects, like some software.

:::
:::

## Quiz: Storage areas

::: callout-quiz
::: callout-note
#### Storage areas

A) Where would you store raw FASTQ files that you just received from a sequencing facility?

B) Where would you store 1 TB of BAM files that you can regenerate
   from the FASTQ files in a day?

C) After three months away, your BAM files in Scratch are gone.
   Why, and can OSC restore them?

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

<!-----
<details><summary> {{< fa square-check >}} &nbsp; &nbsp; _Click for the answers_</summary>

A) **Project**: it's permanent and backed up, and raw data can't be regenerated.

B) **Scratch**: the files are large and can be regenerated, and I/O is faster there.
   This also avoids paying for 1 TB of Project storage.

C) Scratch files that haven't been accessed for 60 days are purged,
   and Scratch isn't backed up, so OSC **can't** restore them.
   You'd regenerate them from the raw data with your scripts ---
   which is why you keep both of those in the Project dir.

</details>

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />
------>
:::
:::

## Storage areas: misc. notes

- **Hidden files in the Home dir**\
  Your Home dir will have hidden files (those starting with a `.`) that are generated
  and used automatically by software. Don't mess with them unless you know what you're doing!

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

. . .

- **Accessing backups**\
  Home and Project dirs are backed up daily.
  You don't have _direct_ access to the backups,
  but you can email OSC to restore your files to the way they were on a specific date.

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

. . .

- **Accessing files across clusters**\
  OSC's clusters share the entire file system, so you can access your files in
  the exact same way regardless of which cluster you're connected to.

# Additional OnDemand features {background-color="#A7B1B7"}

## System status

In OnDemand's "**Clusters**" dropdown menu,
click on the item at the bottom, "**`System Status`**":

![](/img/ondemand_systemstatus_select.png){fig-align="center" width="40%" fig-alt="A screenshot of the options in the OSC OnDemand Clusters dropdown menu." .lightbox}

This page shows the live usage of the three clusters,
and gives a good idea of the scale of the supercomputer center (***next slide***).

OSC buys a new cluster every few years and retires the oldest one,
so the clusters differ in age and hardware:
**Pitzer** (2018, expanded in 2020), **Ascend** (2022, with many GPU nodes),
and **Cardinal** (2024, the newest).
They share the same file systems and mostly the same software,
so for this course, it doesn't matter much which one you use.

----

![](/img/ondemand_systemstatus.png){fig-align="center" width="100%" fig-alt="A screenshot of the OSC Ondemand System Status page showing live cluster usage." .lightbox}

::: footer
:::

## Direct Unix shell access

The **Clusters** dropdown menu gives direct access to a Unix shell on any of the
three clusters.

- We're using Code Server here, but this can occasionally be useful as a quicker
  access point.
- Be aware that you will be on a login node, so you have less leeway in terms of
  memory and CPU usage than on a compute node for testing purposes.

![](../img/ondemand_shell-cardinal.png){fig-align="center" width="60%" fig-alt="A screenshot of a Unix shell opened via the Clusters menu on OSC OnDemand." .lightbox}

::: footer
:::

# Getting help {background-color="#A7B1B7"}

## Contacting OSC to get help

Open a support case in the [OSC Service Center](https://support.osc.edu){target="_blank"}
(log in with your OSC credentials), or email **<oschelp@osc.edu>**,
with questions like:

- Problems with your account
- Installing or using specific software
- Why your jobs keep failing

They are usually very quick to respond!
Include the cluster name, the exact error message, and what you've already tried.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
If you don't have an account yet, use <start@osc.edu> instead.
:::

. . .

<br>

::: callout-tip
### Citing OSC
When you use OSC, it's good practice to **acknowledge and cite OSC** in your papers ---
see their [citation page](https://www.osc.edu/resources/getting_started/citation){target="_blank"}.
:::

# Software management at OSC {background-color="#A7B1B7"}

## Omics analyses use many programs

A typical omics data analysis workflow consists of a sequence of specialized
bioinformatics programs (a.k.a. software or tools).
For example, the RNA-Seq workflow we'll go through:

![](../img/rnaseq-wf-3.png){fig-align="center" width="55%" fig-alt="A diagram showing the steps in an RNA-Seq analysis pipeline." .lightbox}

::: footer
:::

## Getting access to software at OSC

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}

### [System-wide installations]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

OSC has installed a number of bioinformatics programs,
which you can use after "**loading modules**".

But this collection is not comprehensive,
and the most recent versions may not be available.

:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1" style="border-left: 1px solid #A7B1B7; height: 100%; margin: 0 auto; width: 0;"></div>
:::
::: {.column width="47%" .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}

### [Installing software yourself?]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

Installing software like you would on your own computer
is generally not possible at OSC:

- You don't have **administrator privileges**.
- You will often run into issues with **dependencies**
  (other software that a program depends on).

:::
:::

## Lmod software modules

OSC manages installed software with the **Lmod** module system:
much of this software can only be used after **loading its module**
(with the `module` command).

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%" .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}

### [Why modules?]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

It may seem like a drag, but modules make it possible to have:

- Different versions of the same software
- Mutually incompatible software

on a single system.

:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="2" style="border-left: 1px solid #A7B1B7; height: 100%; margin: 0 auto; width: 0;"></div>
:::
::: {.column width="47%" .fragment data-fragment-index="2"}

### [Not everything needs loading]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

Besides the basic shell commands we've been using,
very widely used software like Git, Python, and Apptainer
is available without loading anything.

:::
:::

## Conda and containers

The two best alternative approaches:

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%" .box-blue .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}
### Conda

A software management program that installs software
into "environments" that you can load.

:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
:::
::: {.column width="47%" .box-amber .fragment data-fragment-index="2"}
### Containers

Self-contained software environments that even include
large portions of their operating system.

:::
:::

. . .

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

Both of these:

- Bypass the dependency and administrator privilege issues.
- Make it easy to switch between versions of the same software,
  or to use mutually incompatible software.
- Are highly **reproducible**.

. . .

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
Next lecture, you'll learn to use modules and containers ---
Conda is covered in [this optional self-study page](../bonus/conda.qmd){target="_blank"}.
:::

## Conda versus containers

The two approaches are quite different, both conceptually and in practice:

- **Conda** is similar to OSC's modules, except that you can install software yourself.
- **Containers** are not installed or loaded: you typically just download a file and use it.

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%" .box-blue .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}
### Advantages of Conda

- Once installed, you use software like any other installed software
  (containers need a long "prefix" to your commands).
- A bit easier to create custom environments with multiple programs.

:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
:::
::: {.column width="47%" .box-amber .fragment data-fragment-index="2"}
### Advantages of containers

- More portable, and therefore a bit more reproducible.
- Quicker to obtain --- Conda installations are slower and sometimes fail.
- Conda environments contain many files and can hit OSC's file _number_ quota.
- At OSC, no module loading needed, and fewer commands to remember.

:::
:::

. . .

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
The same set of programs is available through Conda and as containers,
since their repositories are tightly linked.
:::

## Apptainer containers

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}

### [Container platforms]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

**Docker** and **Apptainer** (formerly, and sometimes still, called **Singularity**)
are the most widely used container platforms.

At supercomputers like OSC, only Apptainer can be used ---
but luckily, it can convert Docker container images on the fly.

:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1" style="border-left: 1px solid #A7B1B7; height: 100%; margin: 0 auto; width: 0;"></div>
:::
::: {.column width="47%" .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}

### [Terminology]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

- **Container image**: a binary _file_ that contains the container application
  (`.sif` extension).
- **Container** (strictly speaking): a _running_ container image.
- **Definition file**: a plain-text file with the recipe to build a container image.

:::
:::

## How we'll use containers

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%" .box-blue .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}
### 1. Obtain a container image

From **Seqera Containers**, which has, or will build for you,
containers with:

- Nearly any open-source bioinformatics program
- Any recent version
- Any combination of compatible programs

:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
:::
::: {.column width="47%" .box-amber .fragment data-fragment-index="2"}
### 2. Run the container image

Run a command to access the software
installed inside the container.

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

_We won't write definition files to build our own containers ---
given what's available online, this is rarely needed._

:::
:::

. . .

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
Only free, open-source software is available (this also applies to Conda).
If a program isn't available, that may be a sign it's outdated,
poorly maintained, or poorly documented, and better avoided anyway.
:::

## Other ways to get software at OSC

- **Email OSC Help**\
  They may be able to help with your installation, or,
  for commonly used software, may be willing to do a system-wide installation
  (i.e., make it available as a module).

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

. . .

- **Install the software "manually"**\
  In the best case, you can download a directly functioning executable,
  but more commonly you need to "compile" (build) the program.
  This can get very tricky at OSC due to the privilege and dependency issues.
